name: Pewbeam
tagline: An AI product sold at pewbeam.ai whose exact feature set we have not independently confirmed.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: We have a domain, a price complaint, and not much else: this entry is a placeholder until someone actually opens the pricing page. Products in this shape, a hosted wrapper around a frontier model with a tidy interface and a per-seat bill, are usually two thirds reproducible in a weekend, because the hard part is rented from an API you can also rent. What does not reproduce is the queueing, the retries, the output quality tuning, and the thousand small UI decisions that make the hosted thing feel finished. If the real value turns out to be a proprietary model or a dataset rather than prompt plumbing, this flips to no. Read the verdict as provisional, not as a benchmark result.
coreLoopDIY: Runs your prompt templates against a hosted model from a local workbench, keeps every input and output in SQLite, and shows you what each run cost.
requirements: An API key for an OpenAI-compatible model provider, in .env
Willingness to pay the model bill directly instead of through a subscription
A clear idea of the one job you actually use the paid app for
whatYouLose: Any feature of the real product that is not prompt-in, output-out
Hosted reliability: rate limit handling, retries, and queueing you did not write
Mobile and anything that works when your laptop is closed
Sharing, team accounts, and a link you can send to someone else
Whatever model tuning or evaluation work sits behind their output quality
moatNotes: If the model is theirs, the moat is real. If the model is someone else's, the moat is the interface, and interfaces are cheap now.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because renting an API key and babysitting your own job queue is a worse Tuesday than paying a monthly fee, and because a hosted tool does the boring parts: retries, sane defaults, a UI you do not have to maintain, an output you can show a colleague. Expensive software is often just correctly priced software you only use twice a month. The people who feel the bill most are usually the ones whose usage would fit inside the raw API cost, which is exactly the group a local build serves well.
notes: Thin public footprint, so every field here is a first draft. Someone should open the pricing page before this entry earns any confidence.
prompt:
Build a local AI prompt workbench called "beamdesk". Single machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript for the UI, a small Express server in TypeScript for the API, SQLite via better-sqlite3 for storage, pnpm, concurrently to run both in one command.

What it does:
- Lets me define named prompt templates with {{variable}} placeholders, stored in SQLite.
- Lets me run a template once with filled variables, or as a batch against rows pasted in as CSV.
- Calls an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint. Base URL, model name and API key all come from .env (MODEL_BASE_URL, MODEL_NAME, MODEL_API_KEY). Never hardcode a key, ship .env.example only.
- Stores every run: template id, resolved prompt, output, model, prompt tokens, completion tokens, latency, timestamp, error if any.
- Shows a run history table with filtering by template, and a per template cost estimate using a configurable price per million tokens in .env.
- Batch runs go through a simple in process queue with configurable concurrency, exponential backoff on 429 and 5xx, and resumable state so a crash does not lose completed rows.
- Export any set of runs to CSV or JSONL.

Explicitly out of scope: auth, multi user, hosted deployment, streaming tokens, file uploads, image or audio models, vector search, fine tuning.

Quality bar: strict TypeScript, zod validation on every API boundary, migrations as plain SQL files run at startup, a seed script with two example templates, and vitest coverage for the template renderer, the retry logic and the cost math.

Deliver a README with exact setup steps and one command, pnpm dev, that starts server and UI together. Keep the whole thing under roughly 1500 lines.
